review_basis: Original R2 M07 slides 35-39 checked against spatial slide audit; no old narration or TTS cache reused.
part_title: X-Ray Bottlenecks, Retries, Correlation and Safe AI Telemetry

scenes.title: X-Ray service map for a multi-service AI application
scenes.narration: Begin at the client, then follow API Gateway into Lambda and its Bedrock, OpenSearch, DynamoDB and S3 dependencies. The arrows tell us who calls whom; node labels show P ninety-five latency and fault rate. Look closely at the Bedrock node: its high tail latency and fault rate make it a likely area for investigation. OpenSearch and DynamoDB have their own independent response measurements, so the model isn't necessarily the only source of delay. The explanation beneath the map shows how instrumentation records segments and subsegments, X-Ray links them through trace IDs and the service map makes dependencies visible. The graph should guide investigation, not replace it. A high fault rate at a downstream node may explain failures reported by Lambda, but a single trace is needed to prove the path of a particular request. In a real deployment, prioritise services with both high user impact and poor metrics. This is the point of distributed tracing: understand the causal service chain, not just a list of isolated CloudWatch alarms.

scenes.title: Locate a latency bottleneck with X-Ray
scenes.narration: This slide presents a question-answering workflow split into cold start, vector search, model call, response formatting and final delivery. The timeline totals about eight point four two seconds. One segment dominates: the model call lasts around five point nine eight seconds, roughly seventy-one percent of the request. The right-hand panel proposes several responses. A smaller or faster model may reduce generation time, if evaluation confirms acceptable answer quality. Streaming can let users see the first tokens earlier. Shorter prompts and retrieved context may help when there is unnecessary input. Caching repetitive results can avoid some invocations, provided freshness and authorisation are correct. The slide also mentions reducing cold starts, but note that keeping Lambda warm will not directly shorten time spent waiting for a foundation model. Don't optimise the first interesting number; optimise the measured critical path. After a change, compare request percentiles and output quality under representative traffic, and verify whether the perceived and actual latency improved.

scenes.title: Diagnose retries and throttling
scenes.narration: Follow this sequence from the client through Lambda to Bedrock. The initial InvokeModel call receives HTTP four twenty-nine, a throttling response. Instead of immediately repeating the request, Lambda waits and tries again with exponential backoff and random jitter. The timeline illustrates delays growing from about two hundred to four hundred and eight hundred milliseconds, then longer if permitted. Jitter helps prevent many clients from retrying in synchrony and producing another surge. The right side shows the two possible outcomes: success within the retry limit, or a final failure when the limit is exhausted. The lower checklist recommends recording retry counts and throttling rates, examining quota pressure, and using idempotency protection when retries could produce duplicate side effects. For model calls, distinguish a returned throttling error from a timeout whose outcome is uncertain. Avoid infinite retries; they increase latency and can amplify overload. Add alarms when retries become frequent so the team can address concurrency, capacity or rate-limit policies instead of merely hiding the problem behind longer waits.

scenes.title: Correlate CloudWatch Logs with X-Ray
scenes.narration: This is a practical example of combining logs with tracing. On the left, CloudWatch Logs contains a structured error event with timestamp, trace ID, request ID and error type. The example says an order-service operation failed with a DynamoDB ConditionalCheckFailedException. Copy its trace ID and follow the middle step into X-Ray. The trace map shows the call from the service toward DynamoDB and highlights the failing segment; a later SNS notification was never invoked. The details on the right show the DynamoDB resource and exception. That evidence matters because a conditional-check failure is not necessarily an infrastructure outage: it may be the intended protection against overwriting a record or processing a duplicate order. Inspect the business condition and request data before retrying blindly. The checklist below asks you to correlate the same identifiers in both systems, inspect the failing dependency, apply the correct fix and validate with a new successful trace. Logging the trace context is what makes these two tools a connected troubleshooting workflow.

scenes.title: Safe telemetry for generative AI
scenes.narration: This slide shows a privacy boundary between what a user sends and what operators are allowed to log. On the left, an incoming request may include a raw prompt, credentials and sensitive contextual documents. The filtering stage explicitly blocks those contents and allows only approved operational fields. The example output contains a request ID, model ID, latency, token counts, status and redacted citation identifiers. On the right, IAM restricts who can write and read the telemetry, while KMS protects the stored records with controlled encryption keys. The lower panels connect these choices to outcomes: debuggable applications, privacy by design, compliance evidence and reliable cost or incident analysis. Be careful not to include secret strings even in error messages or exception stack traces. Similarly, storing a user ID as a trace annotation can expose identity unless it has been approved and minimised. The important principle is that full raw content is not a prerequisite for useful observability. Well-designed telemetry captures enough signals to diagnose problems while protecting customer information.
